lines: A Nintendo Entertainment System emulator: it runs a game ROM, draws the console's picture on a screen, brings its five sound channels out as separate jacks, and takes gates for the two controllers
Sets the speed the emulated processor is run at, four octaves either side of the console's own 1.789773 MHz, which raises or lowers both the pace of the game and the pitch of its sound
Scales the clock CV and can invert it, -100% to +100%, before that voltage is added to the clock speed knob
Shifts the emulated processor speed by one octave per 5V at a full attenuverter setting; the total with the clock speed knob is clamped to four octaves either way
A square wave with a 50% duty cycle, 10V high and 0V low, one cycle per emulated video frame of 29781 processor cycles, which is about 60Hz at the default clock speed
Copies the whole state of the emulation into a single store inside the module, replacing whatever was stored before
A rising edge past 2V copies the whole state of the emulation into a single store inside the module, replacing whatever was stored before
Puts the emulation back to the stored state, and does nothing until a state has been stored
A rising edge past 2V puts the emulation back to the stored state, and does nothing until a state has been stored
Freezes the emulation while it is held down: no processor cycles are run and every output holds the voltage it last had
Freezes the emulation while this is above 2V: no processor cycles are run and every output holds the voltage it last had
Restarts the game, as the Reset button on the console does; the stored state is kept
A rising edge past 2V restarts the game, as the Reset button on the console does

Note — the module does nothing until a game is loaded: right-click the panel and choose Load ROM, or drag a .nes file onto the panel. Until then the screen is black and every output stays at 0V.
Note — there is one store for the emulator state, not a bank of them, and each save replaces the last. The store is written into the patch file, so it survives closing and reopening Rack.
Note — Initialize on the module's right-click menu unloads the game as well as clearing the stored state, so the ROM has to be loaded again afterwards.
Note — the emulator reads iNES format files and runs cartridges using the NROM, MMC1, UNROM and CNROM mappers; any other mapper raises an error dialog and nothing is loaded.
Note — CV Genie (Input) goes immediately to the right of this module and writes values straight into the running game's memory.
Menu — Load ROM — opens a file chooser for an iNES .nes file and starts that game running

RackNES.notes: Source read at commit f427150. The installed plugin.json carries 2.0.0, which seventeen commits share; the installed res/RackNES.svg and res/CVGenie.svg hash to the blobs first appearing at d720ac5, and the binary holds no theme strings, so it predates f6bdefe (prototype theme support) — src/ is byte-identical from d720ac5 to f427150, the last 2.0.0 commit before the theme work. MANUAL AGAINST CODE ON THE AUDIO LEVEL: the manual calls each voice output and the mix 10V peak to peak, but nes/emulator.hpp:254 multiplies the sample by 10 and divides by the full scale of a signed 16-bit sample, so a full-scale sample would come out at 10V peak, 20V peak to peak, and the knob can double that again at 200%. No figure is quoted in the lines because how close the emulated sound gets to full scale was not established. The constructor calls emulator.set_clock_rate(768000) rather than the console's 1789773, so the sound library's own time base is fixed at 768kHz; the clock speed knob changes how many processor cycles are run per Rack sample, not that figure. RackNES.cpp:92 declares a PulseGenerator called clockGenerator that nothing ever uses; the clock output is a plain square wave from is_clock_high. processCV runs at every sixteenth sample (cvDivider set to 16 at line 188), and when save, reset and load all arrive together they are taken in that order so the emulation is left where it started. The screen is a display widget with no parameter behind it, so it cannot be clicked for help.

lines: An expander for RackNES that writes values straight into the running game's memory, eight memory locations at a time, in the manner of a Game Genie
Writes to the game memory location chosen in the selector on its row: 0V gives that location's lowest value, 10V its highest. Where it has only two values, a rising edge past 2V flips it.
Note — this module goes immediately to the right of RackNES and does nothing anywhere else.
Note — click the top display to choose the game, and a row's display to choose which memory location that row writes to. Being displays rather than knobs, they carry no help of their own.
Note — only two games are mapped, Super Mario Bros. with 53 memory locations and The Legend of Zelda with 55; the module has nothing to write for any other ROM.
Note — choose a game and a memory location before patching a cable in. With no game chosen, the module reads its tables at index -1, which is outside them.

InputGenie.notes: Source read at commit f427150, settled the same way as RackNES. NO FAMILY IS GIVEN TO THESE JACKS. What each one expects depends on which memory location its selector is set to: 85 of the 108 mapped locations take a 0-10V level and the other 23 are marked as toggles and take a trigger (GameMaps.hpp, and CVGenie.cpp:87 branches on isToggle). One colour would be wrong for whichever set of locations it did not match. OUT-OF-BOUNDS READ WITH NOTHING SELECTED: GameMap starts with gameId -1 and every memLoc at -1 (CVGenie.cpp:48, GameMaps.hpp:194), and process at line 87 calls isToggle as soon as a cable is in, with no check that a game and a location have been chosen. GameMaps.hpp:207-227 then index games[-1][-1], which is outside the table. The source also carries an OutputGenie model, but the installed plugin.json registers only RackNES and InputGenie, and the output half of process is commented out. The eight selectors and the game chooser are LedDisplay widgets rather than parameters, so the census records no paramPos for them and no click can reach them for help; they are covered by Note lines instead. The maker named none of the eight inputs, so Rack shows no tooltip on them.
